stem: A client has a do-not-resuscitate (DNR) order. Which statement correctly explains its scope?

options.A: A DNR order stops routine medications, diagnostic tests, nursing care, and cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
options.B: A DNR order automatically limits care to comfort measures and withholds all disease-directed treatment.
options.C: A DNR order directs that CPR not be performed if breathing or heartbeat stops; by itself, it does not give instructions to stop treatments outside resuscitation.
options.D: A DNR order withholds chest compressions but requires defibrillation and resuscitation medications during cardiac arrest.

rationale: Current MedlinePlus guidance defines a DNR as a medical order instructing health care providers not to perform cardiopulmonary resuscitation if the patient's breathing stops or the heart stops beating. It is specific to CPR and does not, by itself, provide instructions for other treatments such as pain medicine, other medications, or nutrition. CPR may include chest compressions, ventilation, electric shock, and resuscitation medicines. Therefore C is correct. A and B improperly extend the DNR to unrelated ongoing treatment, while D incorrectly separates defibrillation and resuscitation drugs from the resuscitation interventions addressed by the DNR.
educational_objective: Explain that a DNR order addresses cardiopulmonary resuscitation if breathing or heartbeat stops and does not, by itself, discontinue other nonresuscitation treatments.
source_organization: MedlinePlus, U.S. National Library of Medicine (NLM), National Institutes of Health (NIH)
source_locator: Do-not-resuscitate order > introductory definition: instructs providers not to do CPR if breathing stops or heart stops. What is a DNR?: specific about CPR and has no instructions for other treatments such as pain medicine, other medicines, or nutrition. What is Resuscitation?: CPR may include breathing support/chest compressions, electric shock, breathing tubes/oxygen, and medicines.
source_claim_supported: A standard DNR order is specific to withholding CPR during respiratory or cardiac arrest and does not by itself stop other nonresuscitation treatments; resuscitation encompasses more than chest compressions alone.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Management of Care, printed p.20 > Advance Directives/Self-Determination/Life Planning and printed pp.20-21 > Client Rights: assess knowledge of advance directives, integrate advance directives into care, discuss treatment options/decisions, provide education about client rights and responsibilities, and advocate for client rights and needs.
blueprint_topic: Management of Care — DNR scope, advance care planning, and client rights

source_original.stem: A client has a do-not-resuscitate (DNR) order. Which statement correctly explains its scope?

options.A: A DNR order stops routine medications, diagnostic tests, and nursing care in addition to cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
options.B: A DNR order permits comfort measures only and automatically withholds all disease-directed treatment.
options.C: A DNR order withholds CPR if breathing or heartbeat stops but does not by itself stop other indicated treatments.
options.D: A DNR order withholds chest compressions but requires defibrillation and resuscitation drugs during cardiac arrest.

source_original.rationale: A DNR order applies to cardiopulmonary resuscitation when breathing or heartbeat stops. It does not by itself mean that all other treatment, nutrition, medications, or symptom management must stop. Option C is correct. A and B overextend the order, while D fragments CPR into interventions the DNR is intended to withhold.
source_original.source_detail: DNR scope: directs providers not to perform CPR if breathing or heartbeat stops; it is specific to CPR and does not itself stop other treatments such as pain medicine or nutrition. Current MedlinePlus/NLM patient-instruction content live-rechecked 2026-08-15; NCSBN 2026 advance-directive/client-rights relevance checked. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Safe and Effective Care Environment — Management of Care: prioritization, assignment/delegation, advocacy/client rights, continuity/referral, legal scope, professional limitations and emergency/quality-management activities as applicable. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained the DNR-scope construct and key C. Tightened C to say the order does not by itself stop treatments outside resuscitation, matching current MedlinePlus wording and avoiding any implication that every other treatment is automatically indicated or must continue regardless of separate goals/orders.

audit_findings.source_authority: Current MedlinePlus/NLM/NIH content; NCSBN 2026 for NCLEX blueprint
audit_findings.exact_locator: MedlinePlus Do-not-resuscitate order > definition, What is a DNR?, and What is Resuscitation?; NCSBN Management of Care > Advance Directives and Client Rights
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item confines the DNR to CPR and explicitly avoids claiming that unrelated treatments are automatically stopped or automatically continued independent of separate care decisions. No state-specific form or POLST rule is generalized.

distractor_audit.A: Incorrectly extends DNR to routine treatment, testing, and nursing care.
distractor_audit.B: Incorrectly equates DNR with comfort-measures-only care and automatic withdrawal of disease-directed treatment.
distractor_audit.D: Incorrectly treats defibrillation/resuscitation medications as required despite their inclusion among resuscitation interventions.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only C accurately distinguishes the scope of DNR from separate treatment decisions.
audit_findings.cueing: All alternatives define scope; no answer relies on a state-specific acronym, order form, or unsupported technical threshold.
audit_findings.blueprint: Management of Care — Advance Directives/Self-Determination/Life Planning and Client Rights.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Re-audited current MedlinePlus review, DNR-versus-other-treatment boundary, CPR components, all alternatives, rationale, objective, NCSBN mapping, ambiguity, cueing and legal precision. C remained uniquely correct.
